analysis.one_liner: Gives Americans enforceable rights to access, correct, delete, and control the personal data companies collect on them.
analysis.headline: The Online Privacy Act of 2023 died in committee without a single vote: after its April 2023 introduction it sat in four House committees for 21 months with only one cosponsor, until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give everyone in the United States legally enforceable rights over their personal data: the right to see what companies hold, correct it, delete it, and take it to a competitor, plus a right to a human review of automated decisions about them. It would require companies to get real consent before collecting or sharing personal information, ban manipulative "dark pattern" consent screens and forced arbitration for privacy claims, and ban using personal data to discriminate in jobs, credit, and housing. It would create a new Digital Privacy Agency to enforce the rules, and let state attorneys general and individuals sue violators too.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses the internet gains enforceable control over the personal information companies collect, including the contents of their messages. People hit by data-driven discrimination in employment, housing, credit, and insurance get a ban on discriminatory processing, and people targeted by doxxing get a new federal criminal prohibition. Small online businesses get exemptions from most of the individual-rights duties, a nine-month ramp when they grow past the exemption, and the right to reuse approved consent processes, and all users gain because the bill protects their ability to encrypt their messages.

how_it_helps.text: Gives individuals rights to access, correct, delete, and port their personal information, and to request human review of decisions made about them by automated systems.

Requires companies to notify people and get consent before using or sharing their personal information in most cases, and bans "dark patterns" — design tricks that obscure or subvert a person's ability to understand or refuse a consent request.

Bans processing personal data in ways that discriminate by race, sex, disability, and other protected classes in employment, finance, health care, credit, insurance, housing, and education opportunities.

Creates a Digital Privacy Agency to write and enforce the rules, and allows enforcement by the agency, state attorneys general, and individuals in court; the bill also voids predispute arbitration agreements for privacy claims.

Makes it a federal crime, punishable by up to 5 years, to disclose someone's personal information with intent to threaten, intimidate, or harass them (doxxing), and bars companies from blocking or weakening their users' encryption.

analysis.who_pays: Companies whose business models run on collecting, processing, and selling personal information — advertising-technology firms, data brokers, and large platforms that fund free services with behavioral advertising — would bear compliance costs and lose revenue from targeted advertising. Taxpayers would fund the new Digital Privacy Agency. Companies of all sizes would face the cost of building consent, deletion, and security systems, though firms under 200 employees and $25 million in revenue are exempted from many duties.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on companies of every size: even businesses exempt from many duties must still provide notice and consent processes, maintain security policies, and notify users of breaches, and larger firms must build systems for deletion, portability, and public interfaces so users can move their data to competitors.

The bill creates a private right to sue with a very broad definition of "privacy harm" that includes psychological harm such as anxiety and embarrassment, which critics warn could generate substantial litigation against companies, including over practices most consumers would not consider serious.

Requiring affirmative consent for behavioral personalization — the ad-targeting that funds many free online services — could push platforms toward more subscriptions, paywalls, or worse free tiers, a cost that would land partly on users.
Establishing and staffing a new federal agency, the Digital Privacy Agency, with investigation and adjudication powers, would be a permanent addition to federal spending.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real and broadly shared: enforceable data rights, an end to take-it-or-leave-it consent tricks, a ban on data-driven discrimination, and protection for encryption, with enforcement teeth from a dedicated agency, the states, and private lawsuits. The costs are real too — compliance burdens and the loss of ad-targeting revenue that subsidizes free services — but the bill deliberately shields genuinely small businesses with exemptions, a nine-month ramp, and reusable approved consent processes. The sharpest honest objection is the combination of a private right of action with an expansive definition of privacy harm that includes anxiety, which risks turning the statute into a litigation weapon as much as a privacy shield. On balance the design is more protective of ordinary users than of companies, and it died without any of these tradeoffs being tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees the day it was introduced; none of them ever held a markup or brought it to a vote, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Anna Eshoo introduced the Online Privacy Act of 2023 on April 19, 2023, joined by Representative Zoe Lofgren as its only cosponsor.
The same day, the House referred it to four committees — Energy and Commerce, Judiciary, House Administration, and Science, Space, and Technology — which meant any of them could have taken it up.
No committee ever acted: the action history shows no hearings, no markups, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the 118th Congress, which ended January 3, 2025.
The bill therefore never received a vote in either chamber and made no progress beyond its introduction, leaving existing federal privacy law unchanged.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that profit from collecting, processing, and selling personal information — ad-technology firms, data brokers, and ad-funded platforms — came out ahead, because they continue operating under the existing patchwork with no new consent, deletion, or portability obligations and no Digital Privacy Agency looking over their shoulders.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers and ad-funded tech platforms

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew enough support for a partisan fight to form: its only backing was two Democrats (the sponsor and one cosponsor out of 216 House Democrats), no Republican signed on, and no vote was ever taken in committee or on the floor.

industries.note: The bill strikes at the core of their revenue: it requires consent for each category of disclosure, bars selling data without naming the buyer, restricts the identifiers used to link ads across sites and devices, and limits how long data can be kept. These firms profit by trading in information people never knowingly agreed to share, so their interest runs directly against the bill's protections.

industries.industry: Large consumer tech platforms (social media, search, messaging)
industries.note: Platforms would lose the ability to build behavioral-personalization algorithms without affirmative yearly consent and would face duties to delete data on request and support portability to competitors — cuts into ad-funded business models. At the same time, big firms have the compliance staff to absorb the rules, and the bill lets companies keep transferring data to subsidiaries and affiliates, and to foreign entities under negotiated agreements with the new agency.

Firms under 200 employees with less than $25 million in revenue that do not sell data or live off targeted ads are exempted from most individual-rights duties, get a nine-month ramp when they outgrow the exemption, and can freely reuse consent processes approved for larger companies. They still face notice-and-consent, security, and breach-notification requirements, so the carve-out softens but does not eliminate their costs.

industries.industry: Employment, credit, insurance, and housing screening firms
industries.note: These businesses process personal data to decide who gets jobs, credit, insurance, and housing; the bill bans discriminatory processing by protected class and gives people the right to correct inaccurate data and to a human review of automated decisions, directly limiting how these firms operate.
